topic: Seeing Math: The Geometric Soul of Linear Algebra
target_audience: Undergraduate students and advanced high school students

sections.title: Vectors: Movement, Not Just Numbers
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept of a vector. Instead of viewing it as a list of numbers, we visualize it as an arrow in space starting from the origin. This section establishes that 'direction' and 'magnitude' are the fundamental physical properties of vectors.
sections.example: Visualize a small drone at the origin (0,0). To reach a target, it must fly 3 units East and 2 units North. The resulting arrow is the vector [3, 2]. We see the arrow stretch and rotate as the numbers change.

sections.title: Basis Vectors: The DNA of the Grid
sections.content: Explain that every point in the 2D plane is built from two 'basis vectors': i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). These are the fundamental units of our coordinate system. Every vector is simply a 'scaling and adding' of these two.
sections.example: Imagine a character on a tiled floor. The i-hat vector is one tile to the right; the j-hat vector is one tile up. To get to position (4,3), the character takes 4 steps of i-hat and 3 steps of j-hat.

sections.title: Matrices as Space Morphing
sections.content: Shift from static vectors to dynamic transformations. A matrix is not just a box of numbers; it is a 'function' that moves space. Key rule: The columns of a matrix tell us exactly where i-hat and j-hat land after the transformation. The rest of the grid follows linearly.
sections.example: Take a 2x2 matrix where the first column is [0, 1] and the second is [-1, 0]. Watch as the entire grid rotates 90 degrees counter-clockwise because i-hat moved to where j-hat used to be, and j-hat moved to (-1,0).

sections.title: The Determinant: The Scaling Factor
sections.content: Define the determinant geometrically. It represents the factor by which areas are scaled during a transformation. If the determinant is 2, the area doubles. If it is 0, the space is 'squished' into a lower dimension (like a line or a point).
sections.example: A rubber sheet has a drawing of a circle with an area of 1 square inch. After applying a matrix transformation with a determinant of 3, the circle stretches into an ellipse with an area of 3 square inches.

sections.title: Application: Computer Graphics & Animation
sections.content: Conclude by showing how these geometric intuitions are the backbone of modern technology. Matrix transformations allow us to rotate, scale, and project 3D objects onto 2D screens in real-time.
sections.example: Show a 3D model of a mechanical cat. To make the cat 'run,' the computer applies different matrices to the vectors defining its limbs, rotating and translating them hundreds of times per second.
